Would be interesting to know how many of the delayed blocks at slot 1 where after a missed block 0. I'm just taking in notification of the head event from clients. I _think_ that this means that prysm won't send anything for a missed slot, and teku will but only after a certain time (4s?). Yep, Teku will send a head event 4 seconds into the slot with the same block root as the previous slot if no block is received. We'll drop that at some point in the future when the validator client has switched over to the newer way of detecting reorgs. It just all landed too close to genesis to switch over. So <@!144468805697929216>, the prysm node here can still experience the problem but is *much* more likely to get the new head between 0 and 4s than the teku data shows Yep (note too far beyond 12s is likely to be orphaned. it's really the 4s to 12s delivery range that can show this issue) great estimate on % 0-slot blocks in the 4 to 12s delivery range? (from prysm perspective) Give me a sec (curious if it maps to the % epoch of ~3% drops in participation seen on mainnet) ``` interval midpt frequency rel. cum. < 1000.0 500.00 54 36.99% 36.99% ************* 1000.0 - 2000.0 1500.0 54 36.99% 73.97% ************* 2000.0 - 3000.0 2500.0 26 17.81% 91.78% ****** 3000.0 - 4000.0 3500.0 2 1.37% 93.15% 4000.0 - 5000.0 4500.0 0 0.00% 93.15% 5000.0 - 6000.0 5500.0 1 0.68% 93.84% 6000.0 - 7000.0 6500.0 0 0.00% 93.84% 7000.0 - 8000.0 7500.0 0 0.00% 93.84% 8000.0 - 9000.0 8500.0 0 0.00% 93.84% 9000.0 - 10000. 9500.0 0 0.00% 93.84% 10000. - 11000. 10500. 0 0.00% 93.84% 11000. - 12000. 11500. 6 4.11% 97.95% * 12000. - 13000. 12500. 2 1.37% 99.32% >= 13000. 13500. 1 0.68% 100.00% ``` that's a frequency distribution for slot 0 in the epoch. My distribution hasn' t changed much since I posted in the pyrmont channel, but now it looks like: ``` $ ./slot-delay.py 0 count: 1195 delay: 1.97 <0.1: 1 <0.2: 1 <0.3:0 <0.4:2 <0.5:2 <1:380 <2:522 <4:209 <10:43 <∞:35 1 count: 1304 delay: 1.14 <0.1: 1 <0.2: 1 <0.3:20 <0.4:112 <0.5:245 <1:554 <2:264 <4:54 <10:47 <∞:6 2 count: 1299 delay: 0.90 <0.1: 0 <0.2: 1 <0.3:55 <0.4:245 <0.5:268 <1:387 <2:305 <4:30 <10:3 <∞:5 3 count: 1311 delay: 0.89 <0.1: 2 <0.2: 1 <0.3:75 <0.4:248 <0.5:297 <1: ``` for the first three slots So I get <4% of blocks between 4 and 10 and more or less the same > 10 seconds but with only 1000 blocks in slot 0 we can' t do statistics yet This is also a prysm node collecting, just in case it matters The data is showing something similar, in being ~6% of slot 0 blocks coming in after 4 seconds. Yeah i misread what you meant by gap I think there is no such gap with more data. Take a look at pyrmont in logarithmic scale: Yeah, as mentioned could be an artefact due to me not having a lot of data (that was for only ~1/2 a day) But it's also true that pyrmont might have everything shifted, I'm averaging 8 seconds in slot 0 I think that the problem we're looking it remains the fact that block delays for slot 0 are too high, which then leads to the knock-on effect of more blocks arriving at nodes after the 4 second "start attesting" mark, which leads to more of those blocks being orphaned. At this stage I'd be tempted to kick it to the client teams to provide some numbers for when they are ready to serve data for each slot, and when they have completed processing for each block (time in to slot, rather than "how fast did you process this block"). That should allow us to work out if this was a network or processing problem. I think generally, the benchmarks lie a bit when they say "processed block in 100ms" - ie they include perhaps the state transition time, but not the _end-to-end_ time <@476250636548308992> can confirm this, but the way I'm getting this data is by getting the stream of blocks as they arrive from the node and then getting the timestamp from the log event after it's been processed. Perhaps measuring the time delta between these two could be a quick benchmark on processing the block so whenever something comes in on the gossip network, it'll go decryption (noise), deserialization (ssz - heavy because deserializing signatures is expensive), usually some form of internal queueing (because client has to serve many peers), gossip validation (filters out the worst cases, includes signature check), state transition itself, then epoch pruning, epoch finalization pruning, validator balance caching and a bunch of other things, before finally being considered processed Bear in mind we are _not_ after the pure block processing time, but the time between the start of the slot and the end of the block processing process. Because that's the time that can be impacted by internal epoch processing, late arriving blocks from external sources, _etc_. then it goes through the same thing in reverse, but amplified by the fanout of the client: we have to re-encrypt the block for every client because of the unique session key etc so the _first_ neighbour will receive the block significantly earlier than the last This is true, but hopefully the flow in the client is such that as soon as it has finished processing a block it lets the validator clients know that it is done so, and they can start attesting. we have a block arrival metric which we do use to calculate the difference between expected time and 'arrival' time. And then group the results into buckets, although not sure how helpful it is to your cause my suspicion is that maybe clients are taking a bit longer over here ``` [REJECT] The block is proposed by the expected proposer_index for the block's slot in the context of the current shuffling (defined by parent_root/slot). If the proposer_index cannot immediately be verified against the expected shuffling, the block MAY be queued for ``` indeed, we have something similar that tracks that difference, it's actually pretty fun to watch This is a pyrmont node - we can see most blocks for example arriving on time, while attestations are randomly spread around their expected +4s (meaning a significant amount of clients have implemented the randomness fix), then aggregates arriving with some delay nimbus for example starts attesting as soon as it receives the expected block Yeah, that sounds very possible. I have a similar problem with Vouch sending attestations to multiple clients; some of them haven't seen the relevant block yet, so rejects the attestation. If an epoch transition hasn't completed then the block will be rejected. then in that graph, just before 11, we can see how nimbus got blocked for a bit by some processing on the server (a log rotation probably) not sure - we do this one fairly quickly on a hot cache (ie when there's no reorg) - it's an epoch transition away usually from the head Interesting, do you have more data on which clients rejected it ? Ah k, so proposer indexes are precomputed then ? Lighthouse does, I *think* teku does as well but can't remember. It is, of course, an intermittent issue. And to be fair, rejecting it is (kind-of) the correct thing to do. Not sure what prysm does in that situation (receiving an attestation with an unknown head)... "almost" - we can't quite compute them, but we make sure to do _only_ the epoch processing to advance to the new epoch slot without the block applied that's something else - when working with the first slot in the epoch we always do so without the block applied - that ensures we have a clean slate in case the first block is orphaned - for example when storing the epoch state in the database for slot 32, it's stored without the block at slot 32 applied same thing for the epoch cache - it's produced without the block, because the block doesn't really matter for the shuffling and fork choice in that epoch Yeah I want to take the difference of that metric with the timestamp of the log which is immediately after the sync <@476250636548308992> it would be great if the prometheus bucket sizes and count of that metric can be adjusted. Currently it falls mostly in a single 1-second bucket. excerpts.author: arnetheduck
excerpts.content: so whenever something comes in on the gossip network, it'll go decryption (noise), deserialization (ssz - heavy because deserializing signatures is expensive), usually some form of internal queueing (because client has to serve many peers), gossip validation (filters out the worst cases, includes signature check), state transition itself, then epoch pruning, epoch finalization pruning, validator balance caching  and a bunch of other things, before finally being considered processed

excerpts.author: jgm

excerpts.author: arnetheduck
